title: The functor induced by an exact functor is its own right and left derived functor
statement: Let $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an exact functor between abelian categories, $Q_{\mathcal A},Q_{\mathcal B}$ the localization functors of cochain complexes at the quasi-isomorphisms [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], $C(F)$ the termwise functor on cochain complexes, and let $F_D:D(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal B)$ be a functor with a natural isomorphism $\varphi:F_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}\xrightarrow{\sim}Q_{\mathcal B}\circ C(F)$ (such a pair exists by [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-derived-factorization]). Then (1) $(F_D,\varphi^{-1})$ is a right derived functor of $Q_{\mathcal B}\circ C(F)$ with respect to the quasi-isomorphisms, i.e. a left Kan extension of $Q_{\mathcal B}\circ C(F)$ along $Q_{\mathcal A}$, and $(F_D,\varphi)$ is a left derived functor (a right Kan extension along $Q_{\mathcal A}$); (2) the same holds for the restriction $F^+:D^+(\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal B)$ of $F_D$ [def-weil-pbc-bounded-derived-subcategories], [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-bounded-below] with respect to the localization of the bounded below complexes at the quasi-isomorphisms. In particular every complex computes $RF$ and $LF$: the canonical map $Q_{\mathcal B}(C(F)K)\to RF(Q_{\mathcal A}K)$ is an isomorphism for every complex $K$.

proof.text: Put $T=Q_{\mathcal B}\circ C(F)$ and $\eta=\varphi^{-1}:T\to F_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}$. The functor $Q_{\mathcal A}$ is a localization. For every $G:D(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal B)$ and natural transformation $\beta:T\to G\circ Q_{\mathcal A}$, apply clause (2) of the localization universal property to $\beta\circ\varphi:F_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}\to G\circ Q_{\mathcal A}$, with both comparison isomorphisms identities. Both functors invert quasi-isomorphisms because they factor through $Q_{\mathcal A}$. It gives exactly one $\gamma:F_D\to G$ with $\gamma_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}=\beta_K\circ\varphi_K$. Hence $\gamma_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}\circ\eta_K=\beta_K$; conversely that equation forces the displayed value of $\gamma$. This is precisely the left Kan extension property, so $(F_D,\eta)$ is a right derived functor.

proof.text: For every $G:D(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal B)$ and natural transformation $\beta:G\circ Q_{\mathcal A}\to T$, descend $\varphi^{-1}\circ\beta:G\circ Q_{\mathcal A}\to F_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}$ by clause (2) of the localization universal property. It gives exactly one $\delta:G\to F_D$ with $\delta_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}=\varphi_K^{-1}\circ\beta_K$, equivalently $\varphi_K\circ\delta_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}=\beta_K$. This is the right Kan extension property, so $(F_D,\varphi)$ is a left derived functor. Neither argument requires injectives, projectives, or resolutions.

proof.text: Let $(H_D,\psi)$ be the induced factorization pair. The exact-functor boundedness lemma says $H_D$ preserves $D^{\ge n}$ for every $n$. Descend $\psi^{-1}\circ\varphi:F_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}\to H_D\circ Q_{\mathcal A}$ and its inverse by clause (2) of the localization universal property. Descent respects composition and identities, so the descended transformations are inverse. Since $D^+$ is closed under isomorphism, $F_D$ also carries $D^+(\mathcal A)$ into $D^+(\mathcal B)$ and restricts to $F^+$. If $K^r$ is zero for $r<n$, then $1_{F(K^r)}=F(1_{K^r})=F(0)=0$ by additivity; hence $F(K^r)$ is a zero object, and $C(F)$ restricts to $C^+(F)$. Write $c_{\mathcal A}:i_{D,\mathcal A}Q^+_{\mathcal A}\cong Q_{\mathcal A}i_{C,\mathcal A}$ and $c_{\mathcal B}$ for the canonical comparisons of bounded below cochain localization. On a bounded below complex $K$, define the component of $\varphi^+$, after inclusion in $D(\mathcal B)$, as the composite $F_D(i_{D,\mathcal A}Q^+_{\mathcal A}K)\xrightarrow{F_D(c_{\mathcal A,K})}F_D(Q_{\mathcal A}K)\xrightarrow{\varphi_K}Q_{\mathcal B}(C(F)K)\xrightarrow{c_{\mathcal B,C^+(F)K}^{-1}}i_{D,\mathcal B}Q^+_{\mathcal B}(C^+(F)K)$. Every factor is natural and invertible. Fullness of $D^+(\mathcal B)$ makes this and its inverse natural transformations inside that subcategory, giving $\varphi^+:F^+\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A}\xrightarrow{\sim}Q^+_{\mathcal B}\circ C^+(F)$.

proof.text: By bounded below cochain localization, $Q^+_{\mathcal A}$ is a localization for any abelian $\mathcal A$. Put $T^+=Q^+_{\mathcal B}\circ C^+(F)$. For $G:D^+(\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal B)$ and $\beta:T^+\to G\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A}$, clause (2) of the localization universal property gives a unique $\gamma:F^+\to G$ with $\gamma_{Q^+_{\mathcal A}K}=\beta_K\circ\varphi^+_K$, which is equivalent to $\gamma_{Q^+_{\mathcal A}K}\circ(\varphi^+_K)^{-1}=\beta_K$. For $\beta:G\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A}\to T^+$ it gives a unique $\delta:G\to F^+$ with $\delta_{Q^+_{\mathcal A}K}=(\varphi^+_K)^{-1}\circ\beta_K$, equivalently $\varphi^+_K\circ\delta_{Q^+_{\mathcal A}K}=\beta_K$. These are the two Kan universal properties on bounded below complexes, with no enough-injectives assumption.

proof.text: For the right derived pair constructed above, the canonical map at $K$ is $\eta_K=\varphi_K^{-1}$, hence is invertible. If $(RF,\alpha)$ is any other right derived pair, the two left Kan universal properties give unique transformations $s:F_D\to RF$ and $t:RF\to F_D$ satisfying $(s\circ Q_{\mathcal A})\eta=\alpha$ and $(t\circ Q_{\mathcal A})\alpha=\eta$. Their composites satisfy the same equations as the respective identities, so uniqueness forces $ts=1$ and $st=1$. Consequently $\alpha_K=s_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}\circ\eta_K$ is an isomorphism for every $K$. For a left derived pair $(LF,\epsilon)$, the right Kan equations give transformations $s:LF\to F_D$, $t:F_D\to LF$ with $\varphi(s\circ Q_{\mathcal A})=\epsilon$ and $\epsilon(t\circ Q_{\mathcal A})=\varphi$. Then $\varphi((st)\circ Q_{\mathcal A})=\varphi$ and $\epsilon((ts)\circ Q_{\mathcal A})=\epsilon$; uniqueness forces $st=1_{F_D}$ and $ts=1_{LF}$, and $\epsilon_K=\varphi_K s_{Q_{\mathcal A}K}$ is invertible. For a bounded right derived pair $(R^+F,\alpha^+)$, Step 4 gives $s^+:F^+\to R^+F$ and $t^+:R^+F\to F^+$ with $(s^+\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})(\varphi^+)^{-1}=\alpha^+$ and $(t^+\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})\alpha^+=(\varphi^+)^{-1}$. Substitution into these equations shows $t^+s^+$ and $s^+t^+$ satisfy the equations for the identities, so uniqueness makes them identities and $\alpha^+_K$ invertible. For a bounded left derived pair $(L^+F,\epsilon^+)$, Step 4 gives $u^+:L^+F\to F^+$ and $v^+:F^+\to L^+F$ with $\varphi^+(u^+\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})=\epsilon^+$ and $\epsilon^+(v^+\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})=\varphi^+$. Thus $\varphi^+((u^+v^+)\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})=\varphi^+$ and $\epsilon^+((v^+u^+)\circ Q^+_{\mathcal A})=\epsilon^+$; uniqueness makes both composites identities and $\epsilon^+_K$ invertible. Every complex therefore computes both derived functors, with bounded below complexes used in the bounded claims.
